summary.text: Seagrasses are the only land-plant group that grows in the sea, descended from land plants that moved back into the ocean 70 to 100 million years ago.
They photosynthesize underwater, mostly in shallow sheltered coastal waters on sand or mud, and form dense meadows among the most productive ecosystems on Earth.
These meadows act as carbon sinks and feed and shelter a range of sea life comparable to coral reefs, yet seagrass habitat is shrinking worldwide.

facts.value: Ten species, 14% of all, at elevated risk

items.prompt: Divers find thick seagrass meadows a few metres down in a calm bay, but none on the seafloor 500 metres down. What best explains this?

options.label: Deep water is too salty for any plant roots
They photosynthesize, so they need water that light reaches
Fish graze away every deep seagrass shoot
Deep seafloors are rock, never sand or mud

items.explain: Seagrasses photosynthesize in the sunlit upper layer of water, which is why most of them grow in shallow coastal waters.

items.prompt: Before seagrasses lived in the sea, where did their ancestors grow?

options.label: In the deep sea, as drifting plankton
In the sea, as green seaweeds
In salty lakes, as floating mosses
On land, as plants that later went back to sea

items.explain: Seagrasses evolved from land plants that recolonised the ocean between about 70 and 100 million years ago.

items.prompt: Underwater flowers cannot offer nectar. What does the seagrass Thalassia testudinum give the crabs and worm larvae that visit it?

options.label: Sticky, nutritious clumps of pollen
A sweet scent that drifts in the current
Glowing petals that light up at night
Shelter inside hollow, air-filled stems

items.explain: The plant makes nutritious, sticky clumps of pollen that attract small animals and cling to them, in place of the nectar land flowers use.

items.prompt: A coastal town's seagrass meadows die off. Which loss are local fishers most likely to notice?

options.label: More fish, as plants stop using up oxygen
Saltier water, as plants stop absorbing salt
Fewer breeding and nursery grounds for sea life
Clearer water, so fish are easier to catch

items.explain: Seagrass meadows serve as breeding and nursery grounds for many organisms and support commercial fisheries, so losing them would hurt fisheries.

items.prompt: Seagrass meadows cover coasts on every continent except Antarctica. Roughly how many seagrass species are there?

options.label: About 6
About 600
About 6,000
About 60

items.explain: There are only about 60 fully marine seagrass species, a small number given how widely they have spread.

items.prompt: Seagrass roots sit in seabed mud that holds no oxygen. How do the roots survive?

options.label: Oxygen is carried down from the leaves and rhizomes
They pull oxygen from gas bubbles in the mud
They have no need for oxygen at any stage
They grow tubes up to the surface to breathe air

items.explain: The roots can live in oxygen-free sediment because they depend on oxygen moved down from the leaves and rhizomes.

paragraphs.heading: A land plant in the sea
paragraphs.text: Seagrasses are the one group of land plants that grows in the sea. Their ancestors lived on land and moved back into the ocean somewhere between 70 and 100 million years ago. The name comes from their long, narrow leaves. Many species spread outward as their rhizomes extend, forming wide meadows that look a lot like grassland.

paragraphs.heading: Where they grow
paragraphs.text: Like every plant that makes its own food, seagrasses photosynthesize, so they live in water that sunlight reaches. Most grow in shallow, sheltered coastal water, anchored in sand or mud. There are only about 60 fully marine species, yet they have spread across the continental shelves of every continent except Antarctica. Where they do well, they form dense meadows that rank among the most productive ecosystems on Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Pollen that hitches a ride
paragraphs.text: Most species are pollinated under water and complete their whole life cycle there, and their seeds are made under water too. Scientists long assumed that drifting currents alone carried the pollen. At least one species, Thalassia testudinum, proved otherwise: crabs and the larvae of polychaete worms have been found carrying its pollen. Rather than offering nectar like flowers on land, the plant makes sticky, nourishing clumps of pollen that draw these animals in and cling to them.

paragraphs.heading: Built for life under water
paragraphs.text: Seagrass leaves have a reduced cuticle, and their outer skin has no stomata while doing most of the photosynthesis. The roots can survive where there is no oxygen, relying on oxygen carried down from the leaves and rhizomes, and they also help move nutrients. Genome studies show that on the return to the sea some genes were lost, such as those for stomata. The make-up of the plants' cell walls also changed in radical ways.

paragraphs.heading: Why the meadows matter
paragraphs.text: Seagrass meadows act as important carbon sinks. They feed and shelter a variety of sea life that compares with coral reefs. Many creatures use them as places to breed and raise young, and they help commercial fisheries. More broadly, seagrasses strongly shape the physical, chemical and biological conditions of coastal waters.

paragraphs.heading: A shrinking habitat
paragraphs.text: Several studies point to seagrass habitat declining around the world. Ten species, 14% of all seagrasses, face a raised risk of extinction, and three of them count as endangered. Losing these meadows would hurt marine life and the people who depend on the resources and services that seagrasses provide.
